paragraphs.source_en: First, let me begin by describing the disposition of these wasps. Some may say that in a war like this there can hardly be any disposition of forces to speak of, but that is quite wrong. Mention war, and ordinary people at once think of Shahe, Mukden, or Port Arthur, as if war could exist nowhere else; and if they are barbarians with the slightest poetic turn, they immediately imagine such extravagant scenes as Achilles dragging Hector's corpse three times around the walls of Troy, or Zhang Fei of Yan standing on Changban Bridge with his eighteen-foot spear held crosswise and glaring back Cao Cao's million troops. Everyone is free to make whatever associations he pleases, but it is most improper to suppose that nothing else deserves the name of war. Perhaps such foolish wars may have been fought in the benighted ages of remote antiquity. But in these peaceful times, in the very center of the imperial capital of Great Japan, such barbarous conduct belongs among miracles that cannot possibly occur. Whatever disturbance may arise, there is no need to fear it will go beyond the burning of a police box. Seen in that light, the war between Mr. Kushami, master of the Lair of the Crouching Dragon, and the eight hundred stalwarts of Rakuunkan may fairly be counted a great battle in Tokyo. When Master Zuo narrated the Battle of Yanling, he began with the enemy's battle formation. Since ancient times it has been the accepted rule that all skillful narrators employ this method. That being so, there should be nothing strange in my first describing the wasps' disposition. So, to speak first of the wasps' formation: outside the lattice fence stood one troop arranged in a vertical column. These fellows appeared to be charged with the duty of luring the master inside the battle line. "Won't he surrender?" "No, no." "It's no use, no use." "He won't come out." "Can't we get him to budge?" "Of course we can get him to budge!" "All together, bark at him!" "Bow-wow." "Bow-wow." "Bow-wow." After this, the whole column raised a battle cry together. A little to the right of the column, on the playground side, the artillery corps had occupied favorable ground and laid out its position. Facing the Lair of the Crouching Dragon, one officer stood ready with an enormous pestle in his hands. Opposite him, at a distance of three or four ken, another man stood. Behind the man holding the pestle stood yet another, bolt upright and facing the Lair of the Crouching Dragon. Thus, standing opposite one another in a straight line, were the gunners. According to one account, this was baseball practice and by no means preparation for battle. For my part, I am an illiterate fellow who has no idea what baseball is. However, from what I hear, it is a game imported from America and is now the most fashionable of all exercises practiced in schools of middle-school level and above in our country. America is a country forever devising odd novelties, so it is no wonder that it should use a ball as if for artillery warfare. Perhaps it was out of kindness that it specially taught the Japanese this game for disturbing the neighbors.

paragraphs.source_zh: 首先让我从这群马蜂的阵势讲起。有人说这样的战争还会有什么阵势可言，其实这样说是不对的。一提到战争，一般人就会想到沙河、奉天，或者旅顺，好像其他地方就不会有战争似的，一讲到稍微带点诗味的野蛮人，立刻就会联想起阿喀琉斯拖着赫克托尔的死尸围绕特洛伊城墙绕行了三圈，或者联想起燕人张翼德在长坂坡横着丈八长矛，喝退了曹操的百万大军这一类夸大其词的事儿。联想当然可以随本人的便，但认为除此之外，就没有称得上是战争的想法，却是极不恰当的。也许太古蒙昧时期才会进行这类胡闹的战争。但是，在太平的现今，在大日本国帝都的中心，那样的野蛮行动已属于不可能出现的奇迹。不管发生什么样的动乱，不必担心会超出焚毁警察岗亭的程度。由此看来，卧龙窟主人苦沙弥先生和落云馆内八百健儿的战争，在东京满可以称得上是大战了。左氏在叙述“鄢陵之战”时，首先是从敌人的阵势说起的。自古以来，凡是叙述巧妙的文章，采取此类笔法是一般公认的通则。正因为如此，在下要先讲叙一下马蜂的阵势也就不足为怪了吧。还是先说一说马蜂的阵势吧：在方格篱笆的外侧，站着纵向排列的一队。这些人似乎带有将主人诱入战斗圈的任务。“他不投降吗？”“不会，不会。”“这不灵，这不灵。”“他不出来呀。”“是不是搞不动他啊？”“哪里会搞不动啊！”“大家一齐吼起来！”“汪、汪。”“汪、汪。”“汪、汪。”以后便是全队一齐呐喊。离纵队右边一点，在运动场上，炮队占据着已布置好的有利阵地。一个脸朝向卧龙窟的将官，手里拿着一个很大的捣棒在那里摆好了架势。在他对面，和他隔有三四丈远的地方又站着一个人。在手执捣棒人的后面，又有一个人，这人脸朝着卧龙窟直挺挺地站着。这样，成一条直线面对面站着的就是炮手们。据说这是进行垒球练习，决不是战斗准备。我可是个不懂垒球为何物的文盲。但是，我听人讲，这是从美国进口的游戏，如今流行于我国中等以上学校，是最受人们欢迎的运动。美国这个国家是个专门琢磨出新奇事儿的国家，所以把球当成炮战来用，也就不足为怪了。也许它出于好心，才特地教给日本人这种骚扰邻里的游戏的吧。
